lesson.title: Go Back N: One Lost Frame, N Frames Resent
lesson.summary: Go Back N ARQ is a sliding window scheme in which the receiver only ever accepts frames in strict order and uses cumulative acknowledgments, so a single lost or corrupted frame forces the sender to retransmit it and every frame sent after it, trading bandwidth for a very simple receiver.
lesson.body:
Go Back N answers the question sliding window leaves open, what happens when something in the window is lost, with the simplest possible receiver design. The receiver keeps a receive window of size 1: it will only accept the next frame in sequence, the one it is currently expecting. Anything that arrives out of order, even if it is undamaged, gets discarded, and the receiver does not buffer it for later. This lets the receiver be extremely simple, since it never needs to reorder or hold onto frames, but it pushes the entire cost of recovering from a lost frame onto the sender.

Acknowledgments in Go Back N are cumulative rather than individual. An acknowledgment carrying sequence number k means the receiver has correctly received every frame up to and including k, in order, not just frame k on its own. The sender's timer typically runs against the oldest unacknowledged frame. If it expires, the sender assumes that frame, and everything sent after it, may be lost or will now be rejected by the receiver as out of order, so it retransmits the entire run of frames from the oldest unacknowledged one through the last one it had sent. That is, it goes back N frames, or however many are currently outstanding, and starts over.

Trace a window of size 4 with sequence numbers 0 through 7. The sender transmits frames 0, 1, 2, and 3. Frame 0 arrives fine and the receiver returns cumulative ACK0. Frame 1, however, is corrupted in transit and the receiver's CRC check fails, so it is discarded. Frames 2 and 3 then arrive undamaged, but because the receiver's window only accepts frame 1 next, it discards frames 2 and 3 as out of order too, and simply re-sends ACK0 each time. The sender's timer for frame 1 eventually expires. It then retransmits frames 1, 2, and 3, in order, even though 2 and 3 were originally transmitted correctly the first time. That wasted retransmission of already good data is the defining cost of Go Back N.

This design makes sense as an engineering tradeoff, not a limitation born of ignorance. Buffering out of order frames, as selective repeat does, requires the receiver to have memory for up to N frames and logic to reassemble them in order, plus wider window management on both ends. Go Back N avoids all of that at the cost of retransmitting frames that did not need it. On links with low bit error rates or small window sizes, that wasted work is minor and the simplicity is worth it. On long, noisy links with large windows, the wasted retransmissions can dominate and selective repeat becomes the better choice.

Go Back N also imposes a constraint on how large the window can be relative to the sequence number space. With N as the window size and sequence numbers counted modulo some value M, Go Back N requires N to be at most M minus 1, so the receiver can always distinguish a genuinely new frame from an old, already acknowledged one being retransmitted after a delayed acknowledgment. If N were allowed to equal or exceed M, sequence numbers would wrap around before the receiver could tell old and new frames apart, silently corrupting the stream.
